script: [serious] At about eleven o'clock on the night of April 14th, 1912, a radio operator on a cargo steamer called the Californian tapped out a message to the biggest ship in the world. We are stopped and surrounded by ice. On the Titanic, the senior wireless operator, Jack Phillips, was buried in work, sending passengers' private telegrams to a station on the coast of Newfoundland. The Californian was so close, and its signal so loud, that Phillips complained it was jamming everything he was trying to hear. So Phillips cut him off. Shut up, shut up. I am busy. I am working Cape Race. On the Californian, the operator, Cyril Evans, listened a little longer. Then, at around eleven thirty, he took off his headphones, switched off his set, and went to bed. Ten minutes later, the Titanic hit an iceberg. That message was not the first warning that day. It was at least the sixth. And the story of what happened to the others is the story of how the Titanic was lost. The Titanic left Southampton on April 10th, 1912, on her maiden voyage to New York. She was the largest ship afloat, with a gym, a swimming pool, and a squash court, and about twenty-two hundred people aboard. She was also, everyone agreed, as safe as a ship could be. Her hull was divided into compartments that could be sealed off by watertight doors. She could float, her builders said, with any two of them flooded, and even with the first four. And she carried something new for the time. A Marconi wireless room, with two young operators working around the clock, Jack Phillips and Harold Bride. But they did not work for the White Star Line. They worked for the Marconi company, and much of their job was sending and receiving messages for wealthy passengers, who paid by the word. Messages about navigation were supposed to go to the bridge. In practice, they competed with everything else. And on the evening of April 14th, after their equipment had broken down the night before, Phillips and Bride had a mountain of passenger messages to clear. The warnings started that morning. At nine a.m., the liner Caronia reported icebergs, small pieces of ice called growlers, and field ice, right in the Titanic's path. Captain Edward Smith acknowledged it. At one forty-two in the afternoon, the Baltic reported icebergs and large quantities of field ice. Captain Smith handed that message to Bruce Ismay, the chairman of the White Star Line, who was sailing on the voyage. Ismay put it in his pocket. He showed it to two passengers that afternoon. It was only posted in the chart room at seven fifteen that evening, when the captain asked for it back. Minutes after the Baltic, a German liner, the Amerika, reported two large icebergs. That message never reached the bridge at all. At around seven thirty that evening, the Californian reported three large bergs nearby. Bride said he took it to the bridge. And at nine forty p.m., a ship called the Mesaba sent the most alarming warning of the day. Heavy pack ice, and a great number of large icebergs. It lay almost exactly across the Titanic's course. The British inquiry later found that this message never reached the captain or any officer. Phillips was busy. And then, at eleven, the Californian called again. The night was cold, clear, and unusually calm. There was no moon, and the sea was so flat that there were no waves breaking at the base of an iceberg to give it away. The Titanic kept going at about twenty-two knots, close to her top speed. At about eleven forty p.m., lookout Frederick Fleet saw a dark shape ahead. He rang the bell three times, and called the bridge. Iceberg, right ahead. The ship turned, but not enough. The iceberg scraped along her starboard side, opening a series of gaps in the hull below the waterline. Within minutes, the ship's designer, Thomas Andrews, saw what that meant. Five compartments were taking on water, maybe six. The Titanic could float with four. She was going to sink, and she had perhaps an hour or two. There was another problem. The Titanic carried twenty lifeboats, with room for about eleven hundred and seventy-eight people. That was more than the law required at the time. It was also barely half of the people on board. Shortly after midnight, Phillips began sending distress calls. The nearest ship to answer was the Carpathia, about fifty-eight miles away. Her captain, Arthur Rostron, turned her around and raced through the ice. But the Californian, the ship that had warned the Titanic an hour earlier, was far closer than the Carpathia. And her radio was off. Through the night, officers on the Californian's deck watched a ship on the horizon. They saw white rockets go up above it. Eight of them. They woke their captain, Stanley Lord, who was resting below. He told them to keep trying to signal with a Morse lamp. Nobody woke the wireless operator. At two twenty in the morning, the Titanic broke apart and sank. More than fifteen hundred people died, most of them in water just below freezing. Many of the lifeboats had been lowered half empty. When the Carpathia arrived at around four a.m., she pulled about seven hundred survivors from the boats. The Californian's radio operator woke up at around five thirty, switched on his set, and only then learned what had happened. Two official inquiries followed, one in the United States and one in Britain. The British inquiry found that the Californian might have saved many, if not all, of the lives that were lost. Captain Lord spent the rest of his life insisting that his ship was too far away to help, and that the ship his crew saw was not the Titanic. Historians still argue about how far apart they really were. The American inquiry criticised the captain's overconfidence in not slowing down despite repeated warnings about ice, and blamed British regulators for out-of-date lifeboat rules. Out of the disaster came the rules we still sail by. Lifeboat space for every person on board. Lifeboat drills on every voyage. Radio rooms staffed twenty-four hours a day. And an International Ice Patrol, which still tracks icebergs in the North Atlantic today. So here is what the file tells us. The Titanic was not sunk by a lack of information. The warnings came from the Caronia, the Baltic, the Amerika, the Californian, the Mesaba, and then the Californian again. One sat in a chairman's pocket. Two never reached the bridge. One was cut off with the words shut up. The information was all there. What failed was the system for getting it to the person who needed it. Which warning do you think could have saved her?
